questions.q: The six presentations of glomerular disease listed are asymptomatic, macrohematuria, nephrotic syndrome and:
opts: Nephritic syndrome, RPGN and medullary sponge kidney
Nephritic syndrome, RPGN and chronic kidney disease (chronic GN)
Nephritic syndrome, renal vein thrombosis and CKD
questions.exp: Presentations: asymptomatic, macrohematuria, nephrotic syndrome, nephritic syndrome (acute GN), RPGN, CKD (chronic GN). (Book p756)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six numbered presentations of glomerular disease on this page?
questions.exp: The list is 1. Asymptomatic, 2. macrohematuria, 3. nephrotic syndrome, 4. nephritic syndrome (acute glomerulonephritis), 5. RPGN, 6. chronic kidney disease (chronic glomerulonephritis). (Book p756)

questions.q: Match each pattern with its book label — 1) Nephritic syndrome 2) CKD of glomerular disease 3) CKD of vascular disease … A) Ischemic nephropathy B) CKD CGN (chronic glomerulonephritis) C) Acute glomerulonephritis
questions.exp: Nephritic syndrome = acute GN; CKD of glomerular disease = CKD CGN; CKD of vascular disease = ischemic nephropathy. (Book p756)

questions.q: The m/c presentation that heads the biopsy-indication flowchart is:
questions.exp: Asymptomatic urine abnormalities (m/c presentation) lead to biopsy. (Book p756)

questions.q: Asymptomatic urine abnormalities go to biopsy with proteinuria above 500 mg/24 hrs plus microhematuria of at least:
questions.exp: Proteinuria (>500 mg/24 hrs) + microhematuria (≥3 RBC/HPF); proteinuria alone >1 g/24 hrs → biopsy. (Book p756)

questions.q: In the biopsy-indication flowchart, proteinuria ALONE prompts biopsy once it exceeds:
questions.exp: The asymptomatic arm lists two routes: proteinuria >500 mg/24 hrs plus microhematuria ≥3 RBC/HPF, or proteinuria alone >1 g/24 hrs. (Book p756)

questions.q: Fill up: In the macrohematuria 40/5/1 rule, the "1" stands for one ______ plus significant proteinuria.
questions.exp: 40/5/1 rule: ≥40 dysmorphic, ≥5 acanthocytes, 1 RBC cast + significant proteinuria → biopsy. (Book p756)

questions.q: Match each number of the macrohematuria rule with its finding — 1) ≥40 2) ≥5 3) 1 … A) RBC cast B) Dysmorphic RBCs C) Acanthocytes
questions.exp: ≥40: dysmorphic; ≥5: acanthocytes; 1: RBC cast. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: The nephrotic syndrome criteria are nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and extravascular edema; the combination required in adults is:
questions.exp: Adults: 1 + 2 + 3; children: 1 + 2 or 3. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: The hypoalbuminemia cut-off in the nephrotic criteria is serum albumin below:
questions.exp: Hypoalbuminemia: < 3 g/dl. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: Fill up: The third criterion of nephrotic syndrome is oedema, which the page describes as ______ oedema.
questions.exp: Criterion 3 is written as 'Edema : Extravascular', with 1 Nephrotic range proteinuria and 2 Hypoalbuminemia <3 g/dl. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: A 6-year-old has nephrotic-range proteinuria, serum albumin 3.4 g/dL and periorbital puffiness. Applying the criteria box, this child:
opts: Does not meet it, because all three criteria are mandatory at any age
Meets it only if hyperlipidemia is also demonstrated
Cannot be classified until a renal biopsy is done
Meets childhood nephrotic syndrome, since children need 1 plus 2 or 3
questions.exp: The bracket beside the criteria prints 'Adults: 1 + 2 + 3' and 'Children: 1 + 2 or 3', so criterion 1 with edema alone satisfies the paediatric definition. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: Which statement about the diagnostic criteria is TRUE?
opts: Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria were previously part of the diagnostic criteria
Hyperlipidemia remains a mandatory criterion in adults
Children need all three criteria plus hyperlipidemia
Edema in the criteria is intravascular
questions.exp: Note: hyperlipidemia, lipiduria were previously part of diagnostic criteria; edema is extravascular. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria are noted on this page as having previously formed part of the diagnostic criteria for nephrotic syndrome.
opts: True — and they replace the hypoalbuminemia criterion in children
True — the note says they were previously part of the criteria
False — they are the third and fourth printed criteria
False — they were never part of the criteria
questions.exp: Beneath the three printed criteria the note reads: 'Hyperlipidemia, lipiduria were previously part of diagnostic criteria'. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: Nephrotic-range proteinuria by total protein is >3500 mg/24 hrs in adults and, in children:
questions.exp: Total protein: adults >3500 mg/24 hrs; children >50 mg/kg/day. (Book p756)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: The urine protein creatinine ratio (PCR) nephrotic-range cut-offs are:
questions.exp: Urine PCR: adult ≥3000 mg/g; children ≥2000 mg/g. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: Which statement about the urine PCR is TRUE as written?
opts: It replaces the 24-hour protein in all decisions
It is elevated only in minimal change disease
It is not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome
It is the definitive diagnostic test of nephrotic syndrome
questions.exp: Not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: A raised urine protein–creatinine ratio is explicitly described on this page as not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome.
opts: True — 'Not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome' is printed under the PCR values
False — PCR alone defines nephrotic syndrome in children
False — the page says PCR replaces the 24-hour collection
questions.exp: The PCR block gives adult ≥3000 mg/g and children ≥2000 mg/g, then the line 'Not diagnostic of nephrotic syndrome'. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: Nephrotic-range proteinuria is "also seen in" diabetes (m/c), 2° FSGS and amyloidosis; the treatment bracketed for this group is:
questions.exp: Also seen in: diabetes (m/c), 2° FSGS, amyloidosis → Rx: ACE inhibitors, ARB. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: The bracket drawn after the 'Also seen in' causes carries which printed advice?
opts: Rx: Loop diuretics and salt restriction
questions.exp: Nephrotic-range proteinuria is also seen in diabetes (m/c), secondary FSGS and amyloidosis, and the bracket beside that group reads 'Rx: ACE inhibitors, ARB'. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Nephrotic syndrome criteria & nephrotic-range proteinuria · p756-757
questions.q: A diabetic with a urine PCR of 4200 mg/g has serum albumin 3.8 g/dL and no edema. Per this page, the correct reading is:
opts: Nephrotic syndrome, since the PCR crosses 3000 mg/g
Nephrotic syndrome, because diabetes is the m/c associated cause
Neither — the PCR cannot be interpreted in diabetes
Nephrotic-range proteinuria that is not nephrotic syndrome, and the listed Rx is ACE inhibitors or ARBs
questions.exp: The criteria demand nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and/or edema; the 'Also seen in' block names diabetes (m/c) with the bracketed advice 'Rx: ACE inhibitors, ARB'. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: In childhood nephrotic syndrome the edema compartment relationship written is:
questions.exp: Proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + edema; extravascular > intravascular. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: Hypoalbuminemia in nephrotic syndrome arises from urinary loss of albumin together with:
questions.exp: Urinary loss of albumin; ↓ compensation by liver. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: The hypoalbuminemia block gives two mechanisms: urinary loss of albumin and reduced compensation by the liver.
opts: False — the liver is said to over-compensate
False — only urinary loss is listed
True — and a third bullet names impaired intestinal absorption
True — both bullets are printed under HYPOALBUMINEMIA
questions.exp: The two bullets read 'urinary loss of albumin' and '↓ compensation by liver'; the nail figure beneath the Sign heading shows Muehrcke's line. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: The nail sign illustrated for hypoalbuminemia, a white transverse line, is:
questions.exp: Sign: white transverse line – Muehrcke's line. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: For nephrotic edema the book ranks the theories as:
questions.exp: Underfill theory > overfill theory. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: The underfill sequence runs hypoalbuminemia → loss of capillary oncotic pressure → fluid transfer to interstitium, giving periorbital puffiness and pedal edema plus:
opts: ↓ effective circulatory volume with 2° RAS activation
↑ effective circulatory volume with ANP release
questions.exp: ↓ effective circulatory volume → 2° RAS activation → aldosterone → Na+, water retention. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: Which of these belongs to the RIGHT-hand branch of the underfill flowchart rather than the left-hand one?
opts: Transfer of fluid from capillaries to interstitium
questions.exp: After 'Transfer of fluid from capillaries to interstitium' the chart splits: left to periorbital puffiness and pedal edema (extravascular edema), right to ↓ effective circulatory volume → 2° RAS activation → release of aldosterone → retention of Na+ and water (intravascular edema). (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: A nephrotic child has periorbital puffiness, pedal edema, pulse 130 and blood pressure 78/50. The underfill chart accounts for the low pressure by:
opts: Primary RAS activation from streptococcal plasmin release
ANP resistance retaining sodium in the intravascular space
Fluid transfer into the interstitium lowering the effective circulatory volume
questions.exp: In underfill, loss of capillary oncotic pressure shifts fluid to the interstitium; the same shift that produces extravascular edema drops the effective circulating volume and triggers secondary RAS activation. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: Fill up: In the underfill theory, 2° RAS activation causes release of ______, retaining Na+ and water as intravascular edema.
questions.exp: 2° RAS activation → release of aldosterone → retention of Na+, water. (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: Fill up: In the underfill chain, the step that sits between secondary RAS activation and retention of sodium and water is the release of ______.
questions.exp: The printed right-hand chain is ↓ effective circulatory volume → 2° RAS activation → Release of aldosterone → Retention of Na+, water (Intravascular edema). (Book p757)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: The overfill theory is seen in nephritic syndrome; its pathogenesis starts with β hemolytic streptococci releasing plasmin, which activates:
opts: The epithelial potassium channel with 2° RAS activation
The epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) with 1° RAS activation
questions.exp: β hemolytic streptococci → plasmin → activates ENaC → 1° RAS activation → retention of Na+, water. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: The printed pathogenesis of the overfill theory runs in which order?
opts: ANP resistance → plasmin release → ENaC activation → 1° RAS activation
β hemolytic streptococci → releases plasmin → activates ENaC → 1° RAS activation → retention of Na+ and water
β hemolytic streptococci → activates ENaC → releases plasmin → 2° RAS activation → diuresis
Releases plasmin → β hemolytic streptococci → 1° RAS activation → ENaC blockade
questions.exp: Overfill theory, seen in nephritic syndrome: 1. β hemolytic streptococci releases plasmin → activates epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) → 1° RAS activation → retention of Na+, water (intravascular edema); 2. ANP resistance. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: Fill up: In the overfill chain, the streptococcal product that activates the epithelial sodium channel is ______.
questions.exp: The arrows read: β hemolytic streptococci → Releases plasmin → Activates epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). (Book p758)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: The overfill pathway is labelled with PRIMARY RAS activation, in contrast to the SECONDARY activation written in the underfill chart.
opts: False — both charts print primary RAS activation
False — overfill lists no RAS step at all
True — and overfill also lists a fall in effective circulatory volume
True — the intravascular oedema of overfill arises without a preceding volume loss
questions.exp: p757 underfill ends in ↓ effective circulatory volume → 2° RAS activation; p758 overfill goes ENaC → 1° RAS activation → Na+/water retention (Intravascular edema), with ANP resistance as the second mechanism. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Childhood NS: hypoalbuminemia & edema theories · p757-758
questions.q: The second overfill-theory mechanism listed is:
questions.exp: 2. ANP resistance. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: The minimal change disease box states 85-90% with steroid responsiveness of 95%; about biopsy it says:
opts: Biopsy at presentation in every child
questions.exp: MCD: 85-90%; Rx steroid responsive (95%); no role of biopsy. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: The genetic form of FSGS is unresponsive to steroid; its treatment box lists:
questions.exp: FSGS genetic form: unresponsive to steroid; Rx: renal transplantation. MN, IgA: rare. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: Which pair is written in the third management box as 'Rare'?
opts: IgA nephropathy and minimal change disease
questions.exp: The management row has three boxes: MCD (85–90%, steroid responsive 95%, no role of biopsy), FSGS (genetic form unresponsive to steroid; Rx renal transplantation) and membranous nephropathy (MN), IgA: Rare. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: Thrombosis (renal vessel thrombosis, CVT, DVT) becomes a risk when serum albumin falls below:
questions.exp: If serum albumin <2 g/dl → renal vessel thrombosis, CVT, DVT. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: A child with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome has serum albumin 1.4 g/dL and suddenly passes cola-coloured urine with left loin pain. The page's warning that fits best is:
opts: Pneumococcal peritonitis, the m/c cause of death
Renal vessel thrombosis, a risk once serum albumin falls below 2 g/dL
questions.exp: Under Risk of thrombosis the page states: if serum albumin <2 g/dl → can lead to renal vessel thrombosis, CVT, DVT; loin pain with macroscopic haematuria in a hypoalbuminaemic nephrotic child is the classic presentation. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: Listed causes of thrombosis include loss of antithrombin III and of protein C/S in urine, ↑ platelet aggregation, ↑ fibrinogen and ↓ plasminogen; the odd one out is:
opts: Loss of antithrombin III in urine
questions.exp: The book lists ↓ plasminogen, not ↑ plasminogen. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: Match each haemostatic variable with the direction printed for it in the causes of thrombosis — 1) Antithrombin III and protein C/S 2) Fibrinogen 3) Plasminogen … A) Lost in urine B) Increased C) Decreased D) Unchanged
questions.exp: The block reads: loss of antithrombin III in urine, loss of protein C,S in urine, ↑platelet aggregation, ↑fibrinogen and ↓plasminogen. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: Albumin is corrected (to >2 g/dL) using 20% albumin (20 g/100 ml) at a dose of:
questions.exp: 20% albumin: 20 g/100 ml; dose: 0.5 g/kg. (Book p758)

questions.sec: Management boxes & risk of thrombosis · p758
questions.q: Besides 20% albumin, the book notes that these can also be used:
questions.exp: FFP and egg white can also be used. (Book p758)

questions.q: Match each edema manifestation with its severity label — 1) Ascites 2) Pleural effusion 3) Pericardial effusion … A) Mild B) Rare, with disproportional dyspnoea C) Moderate to severe
questions.exp: Ascites (moderate to severe); pleural effusion (mild); pericardial effusion (rare) with disproportional dyspnoea. (Book p758)

questions.q: For moderate-to-severe ascites the book lists ascitic fluid tapping; the m/c cause of death written is:
questions.exp: Rx: ascitic fluid tapping; m/c cause of death: pneumococcal peritonitis. (Book p758)

questions.q: A rare pericardial effusion presenting with disproportional dyspnoea is investigated with:
questions.exp: Pericardial effusion (rare): disproportional dyspnoea → Ix: echo. (Book p758)

questions.q: The dietary prescription for edema is salt restriction below 2 g/day with protein at:
questions.exp: Salt restriction <2 g/day; protein 1 g/kg/day; albumin, FFP. (Book p759)

questions.q: Diuretics are avoided in nephrotic edema; they are indicated only when:
opts: IVC is non-collapsible on USG, because diuretics precipitate pre-renal AKI
questions.exp: Diuretics avoided; indicated only if IVC is non-collapsible in USG; reason: precipitates pre-renal AKI. (Book p759)

questions.q: Daily monitoring of the nephrotic child includes weight, urine routine examination and:
questions.exp: Daily monitoring: weight; urine routine examination; urine protein creatinine ratio. (Book p759)

questions.q: The p759 note lists 'Features against MCD'. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.exp: Note — Features against MCD: RBC casts in urine; hypertension; renal failure. Heavy proteinuria is the hallmark of nephrotic syndrome itself, not a feature against MCD. (Book p759)

questions.q: The steroid regimen written is oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (or 60 mg/m²/day) for 6 weeks with a maximum of 80 mg/day, followed by:
questions.exp: Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (or) 60 mg/m²/day × 6 wks, max 80 mg/day → taper × 6 weeks → stop. (Book p759)

questions.q: Remission (90-95%) is defined by urine albumin nil or trace for 3 consecutive days plus urine PCR below:
questions.exp: Remission: urine albumin nil or trace × 3 consecutive days; urine PCR <200 mg/g. (Book p759)

questions.q: The proportion labelled steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) at this step is:
questions.exp: Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS): 5-10%. (Book p759)

questions.q: Which statement about nephrotic hyperlipidemia is TRUE as written?
opts: It raises atherosclerosis risk and needs statins
It resolves only after albumin infusion
It resolves with steroid therapy, carries no atherosclerosis risk and has no role for statin
It persists despite remission and mandates statins
questions.exp: Resolves with steroid therapy; no risk of atherosclerosis; no role for statin. (Book p759)

questions.q: The HDL fall in nephrotic hyperlipidemia is attributed to:
questions.exp: D/t loss of HDL in urine: ↓ HDL. (Book p759)

questions.q: Match each hyperlipidemia mechanism with its consequence — 1) ↑ lipoprotein lipase 2) ↓ lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) 3) ↑ VLDL, LDL synthesis by liver … A) ↑ VLDL, ↑ LDL, ↑ total cholesterol B) ↑ TG C) ↓ HDL
questions.exp: ↑ lipoprotein lipase → ↑ TG; ↓ LCAT → ↓ HDL; ↑ hepatic VLDL/LDL synthesis → ↑ VLDL, ↑ LDL, ↑ total cholesterol. (Book p759)

questions.q: The associated skin features illustrated with hyperlipidemia are:
questions.exp: Associated features: xanthoma, xanthelasma. (Book p759)

questions.q: SRNS is proteinuria despite full-dose steroid for 4 weeks; the next step, called the 1st indication in a child, is:
questions.exp: Proteinuria despite full dose of steroid for 4 wk → biopsy (1st indication in child). (Book p760)

questions.q: The genetic form of FSGS uncovered on biopsy carries a mutation in:
questions.exp: Genetic form of FSGS (podocin mutation) → Rx: renal transplantation. (Book p760)

questions.q: When biopsy shows minimal change disease in SRNS, the DOC are calcineurin inhibitors given for 6 months with a maximum duration of:
questions.exp: Calcineurin inhibitors (DOC): duration 6 months; max 2 yrs. (Book p760)

questions.q: Match each calcineurin-inhibitor fact with its label — 1) Tacrolimus dose 2) Tacrolimus side effects 3) Cyclosporine side effects … A) Hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia B) Neuropathy, DM, alopecia C) 0.1 mg/kg/day
questions.exp: Tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day with neuropathy, DM, alopecia; cyclosporine with hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia. (Book p760)

questions.q: The first relapse definition in the flowchart is proteinuria appearing after:
questions.exp: Relapse: proteinuria after 1 month of steroid. (Book p760)

questions.q: After the first relapse the cohort splits into no-further-relapse, infrequent relapse and FRNS in the proportions:
questions.exp: 25% no further relapse; 25% infrequent relapse; 50% FRNS. (Book p760)

questions.q: Fill up: In the relapse flowchart, the 25% 'No further relapse' arm carries the bracket '(Very quick ______)'.
questions.exp: The left arm reads: 25% → No further relapse (Very quick remission). (Book p760)

questions.q: Infrequent relapse is treated with steroid, tapered over 4 weeks:
questions.exp: Infrequent relapse → steroid → taper over 4 wks during remission. (Book p760)

questions.q: Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome (FRNS) is defined by:
opts: ≥ 2 relapses within 6 months or ≥ 4 relapses within 1 year
≥ 2 relapses within 1 year or ≥ 4 within 2 years
questions.exp: FRNS: ≥ 2 relapse within 6 months; ≥ 4 relapse within 1 year. (Book p760)

questions.q: The steroid-sparing regimen written for FRNS (to prevent steroid toxicity) is oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day × 12 weeks plus steroid × 2 weeks, or:
questions.exp: Steroid sparing drug: oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day × 12 wks + steroid × 2 wks; oral levamisole. (Book p760)

questions.q: The second relapse line defines relapse as proteinuria reappearing after:
questions.exp: Relapse: proteinuria reappears after 1 month of intermission. (Book p760)

questions.q: Steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome (SDNS) needs ≥ 2 consecutive relapses during tapering of steroid or within how many days after stopping steroid?
questions.exp: SDNS: ≥ 2 consecutive relapses during tapering of steroid (or) within 14 days after stopping steroid. (Book p760)

questions.q: The treatment written for SDNS is MMF 1200 mg/m²/day plus:
questions.exp: Treatment: MMF 1200 mg/m²/day; rituximab 375 mg/m²/day × 4 doses. (Book p760)

questions.q: Adult nephrotic syndrome is summarized as proteinuria with urine PCR ≥3000 mg/d together with:
questions.exp: Proteinuria (urine PCR ≥3000 mg/d); edema; hypoalbuminemia. (Book p761)

questions.q: The m/c cause of adult nephrotic syndrome in the cause list is:
questions.exp: Causes: membranous nephropathy (m/c); FSGS; MCD (15%); IgA; MPGN; 2° amyloidosis. (Book p761)

questions.q: In adults, MCD accounts for about what share of nephrotic syndrome?
questions.exp: MCD (15%) among adult causes. (Book p761)

questions.q: The adult causes grouped under the 'Rare' bracket are:
questions.exp: Rare bracket: membrano proliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), 2° amyloidosis. (Book p761)

questions.q: The adult management sequence is biopsy first, then:
opts: Rule out 2° causes such as paraneoplastic syndrome
questions.exp: Management: 1. biopsy; 2. rule out 2° causes (Eg: paraneoplastic syndrome). (Book p761)

questions.q: The adult steroid trial written is 1 mg/kg/d for:
questions.exp: Steroid: 1 mg/kg/d × 4 months; no response → SRNS. (Book p761)

questions.q: An adult failing the 4-month steroid course is labelled SRNS, whose m/c cause is:
questions.exp: No response → SRNS (m/c: FSGS). (Book p761)

questions.q: The note's Maltese crosses in polarized light and oval fat bodies are both annotated as seen in:
questions.exp: Maltese crosses in polarized light and oval fat bodies: seen in Fabry's disease. (Book p761)
